lessons.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
lessons.concept: In a sentence, the verb must agree with its subject in number (singular/plural) and person. Identify the true subject (not words in between like prepositional phrases) and choose a verb form that matches it.
lessons.formula: Singular subject -> singular verb; plural subject -> plural verb. Ignore intervening phrases when identifying the subject.
lessons.worked_example: Incorrect: 'The list of items are on the table.' Subject is 'list' (singular), so correct: 'The list of items is on the table.'
mistakes: Making the verb agree with a nearby noun instead of the actual subject
Confusing collective nouns or indefinite pronouns in context
Missing agreement errors in longer sentences with clauses

lessons.title: Tense and Consistency
lessons.concept: Verb tense indicates time of action. Sentences should maintain consistent tense unless there is a clear reason to shift (e.g., describing a past event and a general truth). Check sequence of events and time markers.
lessons.formula: Maintain tense consistency within a context; shift tense only when time meaning changes.
lessons.worked_example: Incorrect: 'She finished her work and goes home.' Both actions are in the same past context, so correct: 'She finished her work and went home.'
mistakes: Unnecessary tense shifts within the same clause/sequence
Using wrong tense with time indicators (yesterday, tomorrow, since)
Confusing present perfect with simple past in given contexts

lessons.title: Prepositions, Articles, and Pronouns
lessons.concept: Common errors include wrong preposition choice (in/on/at, by/with), incorrect or missing articles (a/an/the), and pronoun errors (case, number, unclear reference). Read carefully for idiomatic usage and clear reference.
lessons.formula: Check: preposition fits the phrase/verb; article matches countability/specificity; pronoun agrees with antecedent and has correct case.
lessons.worked_example: Incorrect: 'She is good in mathematics.' Correct idiomatic form: 'She is good at mathematics.' Incorrect: 'Each of the players must bring their own kit.' In strict formal agreement: 'Each of the players must bring his or her own kit' (usage may vary, but exams often test clear agreement).
mistakes: Using prepositions based on native-language patterns instead of standard usage
Confusing 'a' and 'an' by spelling instead of sound

practice.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) The bouquet of roses (B) smell very pleasant (C) in the morning. (D) No error
practice.explanation: The subject is 'bouquet' (singular), not 'roses'. So the verb should be singular: 'smells very pleasant'. Error is in part B.

practice.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) She completed the assignment (B) yesterday and (C) submits it today. (D) No error
practice.explanation: The action 'submits it today' conflicts with the past time frame established by 'yesterday' in the same context; it should be 'submitted it today' (or the sentence should be restructured consistently). Error is in part C.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) He is interested (B) on learning (C) new languages. (D) No error
practice.explanation: The correct preposition is 'interested in', not 'interested on'. Correct form: 'interested in learning'. Error is in part B.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) Each of the students (B) have submitted (C) their project report. (D) No error
practice.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so the verb should be 'has submitted' (not 'have submitted'). Error is in part B.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) She is (B) an university student (C) in her final year. (D) No error
practice.explanation: The article 'an' is used before vowel sounds, but 'university' begins with a /juː/ (consonant) sound, so it should be 'a university student'. Error is in part B.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Identify the error: 'The number of students in the class are increasing.'
practice.explanation: 'The number of...' is a singular subject referring to one figure, so it takes the singular verb 'is'. (In contrast, 'A number of...' is plural and takes 'are'.)
practice.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Identify the error: 'He is senior than me.'
practice.explanation: Latin-derived comparatives like senior, junior, superior, and inferior take 'to' rather than 'than' in standard usage: 'He is senior to me.'
practice.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) The quality of these products (B) have improved (C) over the years. (D) No error
questions.explanation: The subject is 'quality' (singular), so the verb should be 'has improved'. Part B contains the error.
questions.provenance: Authored original question; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) He did not knew (B) the answer (C) to the question. (D) No error
questions.explanation: After 'did not', the base form of the verb is used: 'did not know'. 'Knew' in part A is incorrect.
questions.provenance: Authored original question; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) She prefers tea (B) than coffee (C) in the evening. (D) No error
questions.explanation: The correct construction is 'prefers tea to coffee' (not 'than coffee'). Error is in part B.
questions.provenance: Authored original question; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) Neither the teacher (B) nor the students (C) was ready for the test. (D) No error
questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Students' (plural) is nearer, so the verb should be 'were ready'. Error is in part C.
questions.provenance: Authored original question; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Identify the part with an error: (A) I have been waiting (B) for you (C) since two hours. (D) No error
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time, while 'for' is used with a duration. It should be 'for two hours'. Error is in part C.
questions.provenance: Authored original question; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Identify the error: 'One of my friends is a doctor.'

options.B: 'One of' should be followed by plural noun ('friends' is correct) but verb must be singular - sentence is correct

questions.explanation: The construction 'one of + plural noun + singular verb' is correct: 'One of my friends is a doctor.' There is no error in the sentence as given.
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Identify the error: 'Despite of the rain, they went out.'
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed directly by a noun/gerund without 'of': 'Despite the rain...'. (The alternative is 'in spite of the rain'.)
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Identify the error: 'The furniture in this room are old.'
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable (mass) noun in English, so it takes a singular verb: 'The furniture ... is old.' It also cannot be pluralized as 'furnitures'.
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.
